en.CATEGORY: Design tool / Collaborative interface design platform
en.ONE_LINER_2_LINE_SUBTITLE: It does not sell AI. It sells one link that puts design, product and engineering inside the same file. AI is a layer added later, not the product itself.
en.USER_SCALE: Verifiable: the Product Hunt product page shows 4.9, 1,609 reviews, 15K followers and 36 launches (metadata captured 2026-11-18). G2 shows 4.7 from 1,598 reviews, captured directly this run — 82% five-star, 16% four-star, and zero below three stars. Community relay: a Figma forum post citing Finance Yahoo claims 2024 revenue of $749M (+48% YoY) and a planned IPO raising up to $1.5B; that is a community relay, not company disclosure. Figma does not publish ARR, paid seats or team counts, so this card does not invent them.
en.STAGE_MATURITY: Mature. The surface has grown from one design tool into a family: Design, Make, Draw, Dev Mode, FigJam, Slides, Sites, Buzz, Motion, Specs, Figma Agent, plus an open MCP server at mcp.figma.com/mcp. Sites, Buzz, Motion and Specs are labelled beta on the official pages (Sites beta is limited to Full seats; Buzz and Motion are available on all seats). Commercial side runs four tiers: Starter, Professional, Organization, Enterprise.
en.BUSINESS_MODEL_SHORT: Per-seat subscription with three seat types per tier: Professional at $16/Full, $12/Dev, $3/Collab per month billed annually; Organization at $55/$25/$5; Enterprise at $90/$35/$5. These are the USD prices as returned by the pricing page this run, annual billing. Each seat carries AI credits — 3,000 for a Full seat (Starter: 150/day capped at 500/month), 3,500 on Org, 4,250 on Enterprise, and 500 for Dev and Collab seats. Credits are shared across the team; overflow is bought as an add-on or paid as you go. The page states AI add-ons now bring 2x more credits on Professional and 1.6x on Organization and Enterprise.
en.VERDICT_ONE_LINER: It is the default workbench of interface design. The moat is the collaboration network and the file standard — everyone on the team is already here — not the model. What hurts right now is not capability but seat billing, permissions and account safety.
en.VERDICT_BODY_2_3_LINES: As an embedded product it keeps working with the AI unplugged (that was the verdict of my own hands-on test), so the barrier sits in the software and the ecosystem — components, design systems, dev handoff, and the fact that the team is already in the file. The reviews split exactly along that line: 4.7 on G2 praising real-time collaboration and ease of use, while the low scores land almost entirely on seats silently upgrading, duplicate charges with no refund, team admins unable to change file permissions, and a closed account taking three years of work with it. None of that is about design quality.
en.TLDR_1_HEADLINE: AI is a later layer, not the product
en.TLDR_1_BODY: The site now puts Figma Agent and MCP front and centre, but my 20-minute test ended somewhere else: what it replaced was the time spent finding components and laying out a screen — one page cost me 132 credits — not the judgement. Take the AI away and it is still the design tool it always was: draw, edit, hand off.
en.TLDR_2_HEADLINE: The barrier is the software, not the model
en.TLDR_2_BODY: My own note in the test sheet: the barrier is design and prototype editing. That is the mirror image of 007 Framer, where the barrier sat in software too, but in SEO and hosting. It is also why Figma can sell AI as a metered add-on: the core value does not depend on it.
en.TLDR_3_HEADLINE: The weakest beam is seat billing and permissions
en.TLDR_3_BODY: Free blocks the inspector in Dev Mode, paid tiers split into three seat types, and the low reviews contain three independent complaints: outside collaborators silently upgraded to full members and billed for 14 months, duplicate charges acknowledged as a mistake but not refunded, and a Team Administrator who cannot touch a file owned by someone else. These are billing and permission model problems, not design problems.
en.SNAPSHOT_ONE_TO_TWO_SENTENCE_DEFINITION: Figma is a browser-based collaborative interface design platform where design, prototyping, whiteboarding, slides, dev handoff, AI generation and site publishing all hang off the same file and permission model.
en.USER_PROMISE: Official one-liner from the Product Hunt page: The collaborative interface design tool. In user language: send one link and designers, PMs and developers are all talking inside the same file — no exports, no version ping-pong.
en.SEGMENT_1_NAME: Product design teams and design-system owners
en.SEGMENT_1_DETAIL: Solutions pages and customer stories are organised around team collaboration, and the G2 praise repeats the same words: collaboration, real-time collaboration, comments and dealing with the comments are very handy. What they buy is not faster drawing, it is never shipping the wrong version again.
en.SEGMENT_2_DETAIL: A single Professional seat at $16/month already brings unlimited files and Dev Mode (third-party reading, not re-verified line by line here), which is the lowest entry to a professional tool. My own test sat exactly here: one person editing the interface of their own product, with no one to ask for permission.
en.SEGMENT_3_DETAIL: A Dev seat is $12/month, Dev Mode emits code and specs, and the whole annotate-slice-explain loop shrinks. Reviewers on the other side complain that Free blocks the inspector outright — the exact words: Free version blocks inspector mode, now renamed to dev node.
en.JTBD_FUNCTIONAL: Turn an idea about a screen into something reviewable and shippable: editable to the pixel, clickable, and good enough for engineering to build from.
en.JTBD_EMOTIONAL: Stop being asked which version is current. And stop admitting the interface looks bad — my own words in the test: I think what I designed is ugly now, probably does not fit how users actually work.
en.JTBD_SOCIAL: Look professional inside the team: a component library, a design system, a handoff standard — instead of a folder of screenshots.
en.TRIGGER_MOMENT: There is a specific screen already in production that looks wrong — the navigation should be a drawer, the cards should look like finance cards, the whole thing should feel like a real product. That was my trigger, not wanting to learn Figma.
en.FREQUENCY: High during a project (redesigns, new screens, review loops), low in between (maintaining components and the design system). Figma does not publish usage frequency data.
en.USAGE_CONTEXT: Mostly the browser, plus a desktop app. Collaboration happens inside the file through multiplayer cursors, comments and branches. Handoff runs through Dev Mode and MCP. Generation runs through Make and Figma Agent.
en.LOOP_TRIGGER_DETAIL: The trigger is never I want to use AI, it is this screen does not match how people work. My own words: this is a desktop investment workbench, I think my design is ugly now... I want a left-side drawer and finance-style cards.
en.LOOP_ACTION_TITLE: Send the page, state the intent, get a version back
en.LOOP_ACTION_DETAIL: What I actually did: sent the live page that felt wrong and described the target in plain language — left drawer navigation, finance card layout, red-up green-down. It came back with a version built on my own draft plus a node link.
en.LOOP_REWARD_TITLE: A version whose layers you can still edit
en.LOOP_REWARD_DETAIL: My test notes record that it kept the cream background and mango orange, and also kept the empty-position state, the demo-data disclaimer and the risk disclaimer. That is the point: the output is a file you keep editing, not a picture of a design.
en.LOOP_RETURN_TITLE: Next revision starts from the library
en.LOOP_RETURN_DETAIL: Round two does not begin on a blank canvas; it begins with the components and states created last time. That is the difference from one-shot generation tools: the asset stays, so coming back compounds.
en.LOOP_FREQ: Several times a day during a project, weekly across projects ([inference] based on seat tiers and the density of collaboration reviews; the company publishes no frequency data).
en.LOOP_FREQ_NOTE_TRIGGER_CONTEXT: The same trigger returns every revision: realigning which version is current. That is precisely the problem one link solves.
en.LOOP_ONE_LINE_INSIGHT_WHAT_THE_LOOP_ACTU: What it really teaches is thinking in components and states. You leave with parts that work for every future version, not with this one screen.
en.ACQUISITION_LOOP_DETAIL: Three entry paths run at once: public Community files and plugins (adapting something that already exists beats drawing from zero), one person pulling a whole team in, and the design-education and portfolio culture. The third is proven by its own complaint: outside collaborators get counted as members and billed, which means the pull is too frictionless for the billing model.
en.AHA_MOMENT_DETAIL: The first time you see a colleague cursor moving inside the same file and a comment pinned to a layer. After that, send-file-wait-compare-versions is simply gone.
en.VIRALITY_DETAIL_OR_NONE: Yes, and it is written on the pricing page: on a paid plan you can let others view and comment on your files without buying extra seats. Sharing is the distribution mechanism, billing comes after — and that same sentence is where seat miscounting comes from.
en.RETENTION_1: Files live in the account: screens, components and comment history. Leaving is not switching tools, it is moving house.
en.RETENTION_2: Once the component library and design system reach critical mass, new projects cannot route around them — reuse is cheaper than rebuilding.
en.RETENTION_3: Process is bound to the file: review, handoff and Dev Mode all live there, so switching tools means rewriting the process.
en.GROWTH_LOOP_1_DETAIL: One person shares a file, others can only comment, commenters become editors, seats grow. Extremely effective and easy to lose control of: the G2 review about outside people billed as full members for 14 months is the same loop seen from the invoice.
en.GROWTH_LOOP_2_DETAIL: Public files and plugins get duplicated, authors get exposure, more people publish, and Community becomes a search entry. G2 praise in their own words: What stands out most is the Figma Community... thousands of open-source design systems, UI kits, wireframes, and icons.
en.SURFACE_1_ROLE: The product itself. An infinite canvas with frames in the middle, the layer tree on the left, properties on the right, toolbar and collaborator avatars on top. What you design here is what gets handed off.
en.SURFACE_2_ROLE: The object model made visible: frames inside frames, components and instances listed, so you can see whether you are editing the master or the instance. My test could use the output precisely because this layer exists — the layers stay editable.
en.SURFACE_3_ROLE: A reading mode for engineers: code snippets, measurements, component mapping. It turns design-to-code from verbal handoff into something copyable. The inspector it blocks on Free is exactly this surface.
en.SURFACE_4_ROLE: The generation surface: describe what you want in natural language and get an editable screen or prototype, metered in credits. My 132-credit page was spent here.
en.SURFACE_5_ROLE: The distribution surface: public files, design systems, UI kits, icons, plugins. It is the acquisition entry and the default answer to not starting from zero.
en.SURFACE_6_ROLE: Money and rights both live here: seat type, project permissions, file ownership. Most of the low reviews land on this surface — a team admin cannot change permissions on someone else file, and once the owner leaves the file becomes an orphan.
en.ENTITY_1: File (one design file; the unit of collaboration and permission)
en.ENTITY_4: Seat (Full / Dev / Collab; the billing unit)
en.ENTITY_5: Team / Project (the boundary for permission and invoice)
en.IA_LOGIC_PARAGRAPH: The axis is the file: team, then project, then file, then page and layer. Every capability — prototyping, Dev Mode, Make, Sites — hangs off the file rather than a separate shell. The price of that structure is two-level permissions, and there is a hole between the levels: files are owned by people, not teams, so an admin may not be able to take over. The review about losing a whole file when the owner left fell straight through that hole.
en.NAV_INTERACTION_PARAGRAPH: Almost zero learning cost for designers: tree left, canvas centre, properties right, a lineage that runs back to the Sketch era. For non-designers there is a vocabulary tax (frame, auto layout, component, variant, seat). My test did not get stuck on the interface; it got stuck on expressing the intent clearly.
en.CRAFT_1_NAME: Everyone in the same file at the same time
en.CRAFT_1_DETAIL: Real-time collaboration is not a line on a feature list, it is the product assumption: cursors, comments, branches and versions all live in the file. Aligning on a version stopped being a process step, and that is the hardest thing to replace.
en.CRAFT_2_NAME: Components and variants: design as a system
en.CRAFT_2_DETAIL: Components, instances and variants make change once, apply everywhere true. This is what makes usage get heavier over time: the bigger the library, the more expensive it is to leave.
en.CRAFT_3_DETAIL: The most important line in my test: the output was not an image but a file whose layers could still be edited, down to the empty-position state, the demo-data note and the disclaimer. Among generation tools this is still rare.
en.CRAFT_4_NAME: Dev Mode: handoff as a reading mode
en.CRAFT_4_DETAIL: Switch the same file into a mode for engineers and code and specs are right there; add MCP and an external agent can read the design context too. It does not sell prettier design, it sells one fewer translation between design and code.
en.CRAFT_5_NAME: AI as credits, not as a new entry point
en.CRAFT_5_DETAIL: Make, Agent, image and localisation generation all sit on credits: bundled per seat, bought when exceeded. It is a restrained design that keeps the main path intact, at the cost of making heavy users feel every generation as a purchase — my single page cost 132 credits.
en.CRAFT_PRINCIPLE: Get the team to work inside one file first, then talk about how much AI can generate. Every AI feature grows on the file instead of a separate chat window, which is why its AI accelerates an existing workflow rather than replacing one.
en.TTV_LABEL: Time to value: not measured this run (the test recorded sending one page in and getting a usable version back, with no stopwatch)
en.TTV_NOTE_WHAT_HAPPENS_AT_AHA: The test recorded an outcome, not a stopwatch: it rebuilt the page from my draft, returned a node link, and kept the left drawer, the finance cards and the red-up green-down convention. This report does not convert that into minutes and does not invent a score.
en.COG_LABEL: Cognitive load: medium (low for designers, medium-high for others; vocabulary tax on frame, auto layout, component, variant, seat, credits)
en.DELIGHT_1: The generation is editable afterwards, states and disclaimers included — my own note: you can change the layers.
en.DELIGHT_2: A shared link is enough to comment, and commenters do not need seats (pricing page wording) — the collaboration floor is very low.
en.DELIGHT_3: Community files and design systems can be copied and adapted (G2 praise: thousands of open-source design systems, UI kits, wireframes, and icons), so starting is fast.
en.DELIGHT_LABEL: Delight: editable generation + free collaboration + a Community you can copy from
en.TRUST_LABEL: Trust: the product layer is solid (G2 4.7, 82% five-star), but the trust events cluster in three places — seat miscounting and refunds, file ownership, and losing work when an account is closed (G2 wording: my account was closed, resulting in the loss of three years of work).
en.STRUGGLE_1: Seats grow by themselves: outside collaborators upgraded to full members and billed for 14 months; the same file worked on from separate accounts causing duplicate charges, acknowledged as their mistake but not refunded. Two separate G2 reviews, same root.
en.STRUGGLE_2: The permission model has a hole: a Team Administrator cannot change permissions on a file owned by someone else, and loses it outright if the owner leaves. The self-mocking line says it best: I am the team administrator. I guess I contact myself?
en.STRUGGLE_3: Large files fall behind: heavy component libraries and many complex artboards cause lag and memory pressure, and heavy multiplayer sessions can crash a browser tab (G2 wording, on high-end machines too).
en.STRUGGLE_LABEL: Friction: seat miscounting, ownership and permissions, large-file performance
en.REVENUE_MODEL_NAME: Per-seat subscription plus AI credit add-ons
en.REVENUE_MODEL_DETAIL: Four subscription tiers (Starter free, Professional, Organization, Enterprise) with three seat types priced separately (Full, Dev, Collab), each carrying a credit allowance; AI usage beyond it is bought as add-on or pay-as-you-go, and the top tier sells security and compliance.
en.MON_ENTRY_HEADLINE: Free at the door, monetised at the seat type
en.MON_ENTRY_DETAIL: Starter is free with unlimited drafts and free commenting; unlimited files, Dev Mode and team permissions require Professional. The clever part is splitting seats three ways: designers buy Full, engineers who only read code buy Dev at $12, reviewers buy Collab at $3. One team, different prices per role — smarter than charging per head, and much easier to get wrong.
en.FREE_PAID_DETAIL: Starter: unlimited drafts, restricted design files and team capability, AI credits at 150 per day capped at 500 per month, and no inspector in Dev Mode (a limit G2 reviewers call out by name). Professional unlocks unlimited files, advanced Dev Mode and the MCP server, plus 3,000 credits a month on a Full seat. Paid plans let others view and comment without extra seats — the distribution mechanism and the source of miscounting at once.
en.UX_MON_HEADLINE: Are experience and monetisation aligned, or at war?
en.UX_MON_DETAIL_ARE_THEY_ALIGNED_OR_IN_TEN: Aligned locally, at odds structurally. Aligned: collaboration and commenting are free, so people get pulled into the same file, and the charge lands exactly when a person starts doing real work. At odds: sharing is collaborating and collaborating can cost money, so the most natural act — invite someone to look — quietly becomes an invoice, as the 14-month review shows; meanwhile permissions sit with individual file owners, so users feel convenient and unexplained at the same time, on the same model.
en.COMP_1_D1: The same people (the Mac-era design crowd)
en.COMP_1_D2: Local files plus plugins; collaboration needs bolt-ons
en.COMP_1_D4: $12 per editor per month, no free tier (third-party reading, not re-verified)
en.COMP_2_D1: Designers who want to publish the site themselves
en.COMP_2_D2: Own canvas plus own hosting plus CMS; design is production
en.COMP_2_D4: No price on the homepage; four tiers plus add-ons on the pricing page; third-party figures range $10 to $30, inconsistent
en.COMP_3_D1: Teams that need ownership and open source
en.COMP_3_D3: Open-source community and self-hosted enterprise demand
en.COMP_3_D4: Free self-hosted, commercial edition priced separately (third-party)
en.COMP_4_D1: One sentence to a running interface (the AI flank)
en.COMP_4_D2: LLM generates React / Tailwind code directly, source exportable
en.COMP_4_D4: Subscription plus usage with a free layer (not re-verified)
en.COMP_OWN_D2: Browser multiplayer plus component system plus Dev Mode plus AI generation plus MCP
en.COMP_OWN_D3: Community files and plugins, design education, team pull-through
en.COMP_OWN_D4: No price on the homepage; pricing page with four tiers times three seat types plus credits — line items are clear, the total is not
en.COMP_INTRO: The list comes from two places: overlaps inside Figma own product line (Make, Sites and Dev Mode each have rivals), and where users say they actually go in G2 and third-party write-ups (Sketch, Penpot, Framer, the Lovable family). The Product Hunt metadata was captured, but the review body returned 0 items (fetch failed), so this card quotes no Product Hunt reviews and uses only the G2 reviews captured directly. That limit is stated rather than papered over.
en.COMP_WHERE_OWN_WINS: Two things rivals cannot close quickly: multiplayer inside one file, which is a network effect rather than a feature, and the asset build-up of components and variants, which makes leaving more expensive every month. Dev Mode drags engineering into the same file, so the network grows on both sides.
en.COMP_WHERE_RIVALS_CATCH: Three gaps: teams wanting source code and free deployment drift to Lovable, v0 or Claude Code; budget-sensitive or self-hosting teams go to Penpot or Sketch; teams that want design-to-live-site go to Framer. On top of that, the seat billing and ownership complaints bite on money and rights, never on design capability.
en.CHANNEL_1: Community and portfolios: public files, design systems and plugins form a searchable long tail; publishing is distribution.
en.CHANNEL_2: Launch cadence: 36 launches on Product Hunt, 15K followers, 4.9 from 1,609 reviews; each new capability (Agent, Specs, code layers, Motion) buys its own wave of attention.
en.CHANNEL_3: Bottom-up team pull-through: one person shares a file, commenting is free and editing costs a seat — the fastest channel and the one most prone to billing errors.
en.FRICTION_1_TITLE: Seat billing grows on its own
en.FRICTION_1_BODY_WHY_IT_MATTERS: Two G2 reviews: outside collaborators upgraded to full members and discovered by an accountant 14 months later; duplicate charges from the same file worked on through separate accounts, acknowledged as a mistake and still not refunded. Users are not refusing to pay, they cannot see how the number grew. For per-seat pricing that is fatal, because it damages finance and trust in one move.
en.FRICTION_2_BODY: A Team Administrator cannot change permissions on a file owned by someone else; if the owner leaves or disappears the file is orphaned — their words: you basically lose the whole file. The extreme case is an account closed with three years of work inside and no way to retrieve it. For agencies and contractor work this is disqualifying.
en.FRICTION_3_BODY: Big component libraries, many artboards and heavy multiplayer editing bring lag and memory pressure; in the worst case a browser tab crashes (G2 wording, even on high-end machines). For teams running a large design system this is a daily tax.
en.FRICTION_4_TITLE: Free and viewer-side experience are cut back
en.FRICTION_4_BODY: Free blocks the inspector in Dev Mode and long-time users call it unusable now; the viewer side is weak too — designers sharing a link with others expect people to understand the click-through, and reviewers describe a horrible consumption experience. The product is tuned for creators, not for the audience they present to.
en.METRICS_INTRO: No operating metrics are public. What follows separates verifiable public facts from [inference] about what it should be watching; none of it is real internal data.
en.NORTH_STAR_METRIC: Weekly active files times multi-person collaboration events per file ([inference])
en.NORTH_STAR_WHY: [inference] Revenue is per seat and collaboration is carried by files: file count sets the ceiling on seats, and multiplayer activity decides whether seats are actually bought. So the north star is not registered designers, it is people working in the same file at the same time.
en.INPUT_METRIC_1_NAME: Free-to-paid seat conversion, split by seat type
en.INPUT_METRIC_1_WHY: Starter gives unlimited drafts and free commenting; the wall sits at unlimited files, Dev Mode and team permissions. Splitting Full, Dev and Collab conversion shows whether revenue comes from people who design or people who watch.
en.INPUT_METRIC_2_NAME: Credit burn and add-on attach rate
en.INPUT_METRIC_2_WHY: All AI revenue rides on credits (3,000 / 3,500 / 4,250 bundled, add-on beyond). One page cost me 132 credits, so a free allowance lasts about four tries — a high attach rate means AI is genuinely used, and predicts that billing complaints rise with it.
en.INPUT_METRIC_3_NAME: Silent seat upgrade rate and refund request rate
en.INPUT_METRIC_3_WHY: This one is specific to Figma: sharing can create billing, so the rate at which people are auto-added as members directly drives reputation and support cost. The two G2 reviews suggest that number has been high.
en.GUARDRAIL_METRIC: Share of billing complaints plus volume of permission and ownership tickets
en.GUARDRAIL_WHY: G2 4.7 and the one-star reviews coexist, meaning product satisfaction is not commercial satisfaction. These two are the only guardrails that separate design reputation from billing reputation.
en.METRIC_BLINDSPOT: No public retention curve, seat churn, gross margin, or per-credit inference cost [inference]
en.METRIC_BLINDSPOT_WHY: [inference] It sells subscriptions and inference at once: watching revenue without watching unit cost hides the risk that AI gets more popular and margin gets thinner. On the other side, assets lost to permission or account actions never show up in any public metric, yet they damage retention the most.
en.MOAT_REASONING_ONE_LINE: Collaboration network 9, component and design-system lock-in 8, file and handoff standard 8, community ecosystem 8, AI capability 6, price and billing experience 4 — weighted 8. Features can be copied; the team already being in the file cannot.
en.HORIZONTAL_1: From design to handoff: Dev Mode, code layers, Specs and MCP pull engineering into the same file.
en.HORIZONTAL_2: From design to generation and publishing: Make, Sites, Buzz, Motion and Draw catch what happens after the design is done — [inference] a direct answer to Framer and the Lovable family.
en.VERTICAL_1: Product and internet teams: design systems, component libraries, design-to-dev handoff; agencies running client projects.
en.VERTICAL_2: Brand and marketing assets: Buzz for brand material at volume, Slides for pitches — bringing non-product design into the same account.
en.PLATFORM_1: Open interfaces already exist: an MCP server at mcp.figma.com/mcp lets external agents read design context and write code or content; plugins and a REST API are years deep.
en.PLATFORM_2: [inference] The platform strategy is the file as protocol: no transaction cut, moat built from file format, permission model and plugin interfaces, with MCP as the step that opens that protocol to AI.
en.OPP_1_HEADLINE: (My judgement) Show who is about to cost money, before they do
en.OPP_1_DETAIL_WHAT_HOW_WHY: How: when someone is added to a file, show which seat type they will occupy and what it does to this month bill, defaulting to comment-only. Why: the G2 complaints are not about the price being high, they are about not knowing when billing starts. This needs no architectural change and is the cheapest trust repair available.
en.OPP_2_HEADLINE: (My judgement) Turn 132 credits a page into a visible budget bar
en.OPP_2_DETAIL: How: show the estimated spend and the remaining balance before generation, and warn when one attempt would eat half of what is left. Why: in my own test the free allowance ran out with no warning; for a one-person company, predictability beats cheapness.
en.OPP_3_HEADLINE: (My judgement) Decouple file ownership from the individual
en.OPP_3_DETAIL: How: let team admins take over files and permissions from departing members, and prompt an export when an account is deactivated. Why: the review about a closed account destroying three years of work is the most expensive kind of failure — it costs not one user but that person entire body of work and every recommendation they would have made.
en.STRATEGIC_HEADLINE: The bet: lock the team with collaboration, then swallow everything after the design
en.STRATEGIC_DETAIL_HIGH_IMPACT_BET: Two bets at once. One: hang design, handoff, generation and publishing off the same file (Dev Mode, MCP, Make, Sites) so that switching tools means switching how the team works. Two: keep AI as a metered add-on rather than a replacement for the main path. The first hardens the moat, the second protects margin — and together they guarantee the question of why the bill is this high stays open, because the more AI people use, the harder the invoice is to explain.
en.MOONSHOT_HEADLINE: Endgame: remove handoff as a step
en.MOONSHOT_DETAIL_WHY_IT_COULD_RESHAPE_THE: If an agent can read design intent, produce maintainable components and emit both code and specs, the three translations between designer, engineer and PM collapse into one. The distance is not model quality, it is who signs off — my test already found that it does not correct a wrong premise, judgement stays human. The endgame bottleneck is trust and accountability, not generation.
en.RISK_INTRO: Risks ordered by likelihood times impact. Severity is my judgement, not company disclosure.
en.RISK_1_NAME: Seat and credit billing keeps eroding trust
en.RISK_1_MIT: Show seat type and cost at the moment of joining, default to comment-only, and auto-refund acknowledged billing errors. Without this, higher ARPU means worse reputation, eventually papered over by enterprise contracts.
en.RISK_2_MIT: Team-level takeover, export prompts before deactivation, an appeal and retrieval window before suspension. For agencies and contractor workflows this decides stay or leave.
en.RISK_3_NAME: Code-first AI tools route around it
en.RISK_3_MIT: Defend editable output, component accumulation and the handoff chain; treat MCP and code layers as entry points rather than threats. The real danger is a new team starting from code and never entering a design tool at all.
en.RISK_4_NAME: Large-file performance and viewer experience drag reputation
en.RISK_4_MIT: Offer a performance profile for huge design systems (chunked loading, read-only mode) and a separate presentation experience for non-designers — that is where decision makers meet the product first.

en.SHOT_2_CAPTION: Figma Make: generate an interface from natural language, chat and code on the left, preview on the right (official hero from figma.com/make)
en.SHOT_3_CAPTION: Dev Mode: the same file switched into an engineering view with code layers and mobile specs (official hero from figma.com/dev-mode)
en.SHOT_4_CAPTION: Figma AI: panels for code generation and prompt enhancement (official hero from figma.com/ai)
en.SHOT_5_CAPTION: Figma Motion: motion editing with a timeline next to the canvas (official hero from figma.com/motion)
en.SHOT_6_CAPTION: A mobile frame with the settings panel on the right: homepage image showing layers and properties on a phone-sized artboard (from figma.com)
en.AGENTIC_CANDIDATE_1: Figma Agent: central to both the official narrative and the 2026-10-07 Product Hunt launch; it reads in-file context and acts on the design.
en.AGENTIC_CANDIDATE_2: Make plus code layers: from a sentence to a working interface, then to shippable code layers — generation and handoff joined (PH launch 2026-10-23: Figma code layers).
en.AGENTIC_CANDIDATE_3: [inference] The MCP server is the real agentic step: once Claude, Cursor or Codex can read design context and write back, Figma becomes the database of design state rather than a screen-drawing tool.
en.AI_DISRUPTION_RISK: Two paths. Code-first generation tools can mean new teams never enter a design tool at all, which threatens the increment. And AI devalues drawing the screen itself, pushing value toward component governance, handoff and collaboration — which is where Figma already charges, so the threat is structural but slow.
en.AI_OPPORTUNITY_1: (My judgement) Make generate, review and handoff one chain with diffs: every agent change lists which components and states moved, so a human reviews instead of searching.
en.AI_OPPORTUNITY_2: (My judgement) Feed the design system to the agent as a constraint, so it must build from existing components instead of improvising — the layer design-system teams would pay for most readily.
en.ASSUMPTIONS_ONE_PARAGRAPH_LIST_WHAT_IS_I: Verifiable: product line and beta labels, four pricing tiers with three seat types in USD at annual billing, per-seat credit allowances and add-on rules, the MCP endpoint, Product Hunt product metadata (4.9, 1,609, 15K, 36 launches), G2 4.7 from 1,598 reviews with 10 low-rated quotes captured directly, and my own 20-minute test record. Inferred and marked: revenue and IPO figures (community relay via Finance Yahoo), retention and seat churn, margin structure, competitor prices (third-party and mutually inconsistent), and the choice of north star and guardrail metrics.
en.ASSUMPTION_1: [inference] The pricing page returned USD list prices on annual billing; third-party write-ups also quote $20 monthly for a single seat that includes unlimited files and Dev Mode. Both readings circulate, so this card follows the official page and treats the rest as order-of-magnitude only.
en.ASSUMPTION_2: [inference] The paying core is one to three people who actually design plus many who only comment: three seat types with free commenting only makes sense in that team shape, and it explains why seats get upgraded silently.
en.CATEGORY_POSITIONING_PARAGRAPH: It sits where two shelves cross: design tools (Sketch, Penpot) and design-to-web builders (Framer, Webflow), plus AI generation (Lovable, v0). On the shelf it leans design but further toward collaboration and handoff: more than a design tool because of Dev Mode and Community, less than a site builder because it does not own publishing or deep SEO, and more than a generation tool because the output stays maintainable.
en.CURRENT_AI_USAGE_PARAGRAPH: AI appears in four places: Make for generating editable interfaces from language, Figma Agent for acting inside the file, image and localisation generation metered in credits, and MCP for external agents. My test used the Make and Agent path: send a live page, state the intent, get an editable version back at 132 credits.
en.FINAL_BREAKS: Teams that need source-code ownership and self-deployment (they go to Lovable, v0, Claude Code); anyone on a tight budget or needing self-hosting (Penpot); teams that only want design-to-live-site (Framer); and agencies where ownership safety is a hard requirement — losing a file because the owner left is enough to lose the deal.
en.FINAL_MOAT_OR_LACK_THEREOF: The moat is real and very specifically located: not the model, but collaboration network plus component accumulation plus handoff standard. The first two are built out of time and habit, the third is an industry default. AI only reinforced a small piece of the third, so the moat will not be closed by a better model — it can only be routed around if new teams start from code and never adopt a design tool.
en.FINAL_WINS: Multiplayer in one file as a network effect, components and design systems as accumulating assets, Dev Mode pulling handoff into the same file, and Community plus plugins as a distribution long tail.
en.SIX_INTRO: Six dimensions of the application layer: not how many AI features it has, but which step it removes and what mess it hands back. Evidence: a 20-minute hands-on test on 2026-11-18, official site and pricing page text, and G2 reviews captured directly.
en.AI_TYPE_REASON: Unplug test: remove the AI and Figma is still a complete design and collaboration tool — draw, edit, comment, hand off. So the type is embedded, not AI-native. AI shows up in four places (Make, Agent, image generation, MCP) while the main path stays the file and the canvas.
en.SIX_1: It removes the most tiring part of turning an idea into a reviewable screen: finding components, laying out the frame, aligning states. Designers did this before and still do it now, but several rounds collapse into one generation plus edits; the cost moves from hours to a $16 subscription plus 132 credits a go. My own words in the test: what it saves is the designer hunting for components and templates.
en.SIX_2: It chews through about half the dirty work: page structure, state preservation, colour system, disclaimers — anything that means follow my draft — it handles. What it hands back is the designer judgement itself. So the user must state the intent clearly (left drawer, finance cards, red-up green-down); if you cannot, it cannot build it right. That barrier belongs to expression and taste, not to software.
en.SIX_3: Usable. My test verdict: usable, the layers can be edited. But would anyone publish it as is — no, I still think it needs a professional. It returns workable material, not a final draft.
en.SIX_4: The safety net is thin: it flags that the data is fake and needs a real feed, but a wrong premise from the user is not its problem (my note: it does not care about that) — it will build on it and mention that it is opening a new page. No source labels, no confidence, and the check stays human.
en.SIX_5: Cheap to be wrong. The structure breaks down to layers, changes can be undone, history exists (my note: undo works). The real cost is credits: one page was 132, so a free allowance lasts about four attempts. Here, cost of error is quota, not data loss.
en.SIX_6: Replaceable, but habit stays. My own words: replaceable, but the habit is there — compared with Framer it leans more toward accumulating design material and can export code prototypes; plugins are callable but capped in number. If Figma disappeared tomorrow, the substitute is the designer.
